paragraphs.source_en: The coexistence of groups with two different economies, namely hunting and herding, could have had mutual influence and could have generated a new set of social relations. Since in the excavated shelters only a pastoral economy is attested to after 7,500 BP, it raises the question of whether the hunter-gatherers became pastoralists or whether they moved elsewhere. A survey near the Erg Titersin next to the Acacus Mountains provided archaeological evidence for a lacustrine adaptation by the hunters during the Pastoral phase (Cremaschi & Di Lernia 2001). This evidence suggests that the onset of domesticated cattle in the Central Sahara did not mean the end of hunting and gathering and the term "Pastoral phase" should not therefore be considered as the synonym for an exclusive economy in the whole region.

paragraphs.source_en: This fact is further confirmed by the ancient literature. Herodotus (1899) describes how Garamantes slaughtered troglodytes, whom they found living in the Libyan desert. The Garamantes were powerful Saharan people of Berber origin who lived in Fezzan northeast of the Acacus between 2,500 BP and 1,500 BP. The identity of these troglodytes is not known and Herodotus gave only three notes about them; they were hunters feeding on small reptiles, they run very quickly so that the Garamantes had to use horses and chariots to catch them; and their language was not comprehensible to anyone as they "screech like bats" (Herodotus 1899: 268). The fundamental piece of information is that hunter-gatherers still lived in the Central Sahara after the Pastoral phase, namely during the successive Caballine period when the region was already very arid and the population was concentrated in the oasis.
